result:
**Pick PostgreSQL, with a `jsonb` column for the varied attributes.** You get the flexible-schema benefit that draws people to MongoDB, without giving up relational features a catalogue ends up needing.

| Concern | PostgreSQL (+ `jsonb`) | MongoDB |
|---|---|---|
| Varied attributes per product | `attributes jsonb` column; a GIN index covers containment queries on any key | Native document model; slightly more ergonomic |
| Fixed fields (SKU, price, category, stock) | Real columns with types, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK` and foreign keys | Optional JSON Schema validation; no foreign keys |
| Relations (categories, brands, variants, orders, inventory) | Joins and foreign keys | `$lookup` works but is clumsier; you usually denormalise and keep copies in sync yourself |
| Transactions | Mature, on by default | Multi-document transactions exist but with more caveats and overhead |
| Faceted filtering on arbitrary attributes | GIN handles equality/containment; range queries on a JSON key need a per-key expression index | Wildcard indexes cover arbitrary keys, including ranges; a little better here |
| Reporting and ad-hoc queries | SQL, and every BI tool speaks it | Aggregation pipeline; fewer tools, steeper learning curve |
| Horizontal write scaling | Single primary plus read replicas; sharding needs Citus or similar | Built-in sharding |
| Search | Built-in full-text is adequate | Similar natively; Atlas Search is good but Atlas-only |

**Why PostgreSQL wins here**
- A catalogue is only partly schemaless. The core is fixed and relational (SKU, price, category, stock), and only the long tail of attributes varies, which is the shape that columns plus `jsonb` fits.
- The catalogue will be joined to orders, inventory and pricing, where integrity constraints and transactions are worth having.
- Catalogues are read-heavy and rarely huge. Millions of products sit comfortably on one Postgres node with replicas, so MongoDB's sharding advantage is unlikely to matter.

**When I would pick MongoDB instead**
- The products really are deeply nested, heterogeneous documents with almost no shared fields and no relations to other data.
- You expect write volume or data size beyond a single node from early on.
- The team already runs MongoDB in production and has no Postgres experience.

A minimal starting shape:

```sql
CREATE TABLE product (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  category_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES category(id),
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
  attributes  jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);
CREATE INDEX product_attributes_idx ON product USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops);
```

Promote an attribute to a real column once you find yourself filtering or sorting on it everywhere.
